Chapter 2
Corporate Opacity and Financial Visibility under Sanctions.

The share of eligible firms with a public statement rose from 2021 to 2024. This chapter shows which firms stay visible in the archive and where the others went.

Where firms went State-related firms Industries The opacity index Size Firms followed Finances The sanctions list Keeping and regaining The map

A missing statement precedes exit more often than a return to publication.

Each dot represents about 2,000 firms, starting with 3.4 million eligible firms registered at the end of 2019. Across all one-year transitions ending in 2020 to 2024 that began without a statement, 29.1% ended in removal from the register and 9.6% ended with a statement. Removal was three times as common as a return to publication.

This is why the share of all eligible firms with a statement rose through 2024. The register lost 1.7 million firms from 2020 to 2024, most of them firms without statements, while the number of firms with statements held.

The fall among state-related firms is mostly registry exit, concentrated in one legal form and one year.

From 2021 to 2024 the share with a statement fell from 69.8% to 61.3% among state-related firms, while it rose among private firms and among firms with foreign or joint ownership. The fall is in one legal form. Among state and municipal enterprises, which operate publicly owned assets and issue no shares, the share went from 69.2% to 48.2%.

Most of that fall is exit from the register. Of these enterprises, 83.2% were removed during 2024. The exits coincide with the original 1 January 2025 deadline to liquidate or reorganize such enterprises in competitive markets, subject to statutory exceptions. A December 2024 amendment allowed completion by 31 December 2025 where the founder had made the required decision before the original deadline. Among state-related firms still registered at year-end, the share with a statement was 75.8% in 2021 and 76.1% in 2024.

One group did lose statements while staying registered. Among the 14,256 firms that were state-related at the end of both years, the share fell from 80.4% to 74.2%.

Across industries the rise was broad.

From 2021 to 2024 the share with a statement rose in 19 of the 20 largest industries. It rose from 61.0% to 65.4% in wholesale trade, from 56.4% to 59.2% in building construction, and from 71.2% to 74.0% in real estate. The industries are fixed across years, so each row compares the same industry, though not the same firms within it.

The opacity index describes the return to withholding financial information.

A firm weighs what opacity protects against what it costs. Public statements can inform sanctions enforcement, so enforcement pressure raises the benefit of withholding them. Customers, suppliers, and lenders may decline business they cannot verify, so the cost of opacity rises with the business a firm has at stake, and it is lower for a firm entitled to withhold its accounts. The curve turns that balance into the probability that a statement is available. The slider settings are illustrations, and the estimates are in the two figures that follow.

Model quantityEffectCounterpart in the data
Enforcement pressure, eraises the benefit of opacitymembership of the sanctions list
Entitlement to withhold information, Elowers the cost of opacitymembership of the 2020 filing-exemption list
Counterparty business at stake, ψraises the cost of opacitytotal assets in the preceding year

The entitlement shows directly in the archive. None of the 22 eligible firms on the 2020 filing-exemption list has an available statement for any year from 2019 to 2023.

In the dissertation: Section 2.3, Table A.3, Section 2.6.1

The firms whose statements stay public are the larger ones.

Among firms that had a statement the year before and remained eligible and registered, a statement remained available in 2022 for 95.1% of firms in the highest fifth by assets and for 83.9% in the lowest, an observed gap of 11.1 percentage points. With the registry characteristics held constant, the odds of continued availability were 3.84 times as high in the highest fifth as in the lowest, and between 3.21 and 3.90 times in each year from 2020 to 2024. In 2014 to 2018 the same ratio lay between 2.31 and 2.48.

In the opacity index a larger firm has more business with counterparties that require public accounts, which raises its cost of opacity. Smaller firms are also the firms most likely to be winding down, and the comparison cannot separate the two.

The same ordering appears when firms are followed from before the invasion.

Of the firms with a statement in each of 2019, 2020, and 2021, 4.8% of those in the lowest fifth by 2021 assets remained eligible and registered through 2024 and had no statement in any of 2022, 2023, or 2024. The share falls with size, to 2.0% in the highest fifth. Here each firm keeps its 2021 fifth and is followed for three years, where the yearly comparison above forms the fifths anew each year.

By ownership the share is 3.4% for firms with foreign or joint ownership, 2.8% for private firms, and 1.6% for state-related firms.

Size, profitability, and liquidity all predict continued availability when they enter together.

In the common sample with all three financial measures recorded, 94.3% of observations have a statement for the following year. At that starting probability, the estimates correspond to illustrative increases of about 0.6 percentage points for a doubling of assets, 0.1 points for ten points more operating margin, and 0.4 points for ten points more cash share.

With all three measures entered and the registry characteristics held constant, doubling total assets is associated with 12.9% higher odds of a statement the following year (95% confidence interval, 11.3% to 14.6%). Ten percentage points more operating margin and ten points more cash share are associated with 2.5% and 7.1% higher odds. All three coefficients are statistically significant at the 1% level.

The cash share predicts availability only with size and profitability held constant. Entered alone, its estimate is 1.6% and is not statistically significant at the 5% level, the pattern expected if firms with high cash shares tend to be small.

Firms on the sanctions list moved from more visible than comparable firms to less visible.

The predicted probability of an available statement for firms on the sanctions list and no other list was 1.1 percentage points below that of comparable firms on no list for 2021 and 12.6 points below it for 2024. The comparison holds the registry characteristics constant and list membership fixed across years. Their odds of an available statement were 2.88 times those of firms on no list in 2013 and 43.0% lower in 2024 (95% confidence interval, 10.3% to 63.7% lower). In 2025* they were 46.3% lower. The two periods are estimated in separate models, and the 2019 value is affected by the change of provider.

In the opacity model, greater enforcement pressure raises the benefit of withholding statements. The decline is consistent with firms on the sanctions list using the access restrictions, although the archive does not identify each firm's reason for absence. Firms on the government's strategic list are rarely visible in any year: the predicted probability of an available statement was 6.5% for 2024, against 68.6% for firms on no list.

Sanctioned firms did not withdraw uniformly.

Among firms that had a statement the year before, those on the sanctions list were more likely than comparable firms to keep it (odds ratio 1.73). Sanctioned firms without one were far less likely than comparable firms to regain it (odds ratio 0.17). Both states were more persistent for sanctioned firms.

The histories of individual firms show the same split. Of the sanctioned firms eligible and registered at the end of 2019, 3.52% had a statement in each of 2019, 2020, and 2021 and none in 2022, 2023, or 2024 while remaining registered, against 1.31% of firms on no list.

In the dissertation: Section 2.6.2, Table 2.5, Table B.10

Among located firms the share with a statement rose in line with the national figure.

Of the firms eligible in 2021, 3,277,638 have coordinates. Among eligible firms with coordinates in each year, 64.0% had a statement in 2021 and 66.5% in 2024. The Visibility Atlas maps firms at their registered addresses, year by year, and the film Who stays visible? follows the same data.
